name: Republic of Paraguay (Francisco Solano Lopez)

areaKm2.note: world_1815 polygon "Paraguay" = about 348,900 km2 on the sphere (pre-war Paraguay with its Chaco and Misiones claims; the polygon is unchanged in world_1783 and world_1800). Low: the post-war world_1878/1880 polygon, about 270,400 km2, after the cessions of 1872-76. Basemap borders are approximate and the pre-war frontiers were disputed.

population.note: Pre-war (1864) estimates: Whigham and Potthast 1999 420,000-450,000 (mid); Reber 1988 about 300,000 (low); Williams 1976 about 407,000, range 373,000-575,000 by assumed growth rate (high). Salles 2003 p. 18 gives about 450,000 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguayan_War). The traditional 1.3 million rests on an 1857 census Reber shows never took place and is not used.

urbanization.note: Educated guess: Asuncion was the only town of any size; the rest of the population lived in rural partidos and small river towns.

activePersonnel.note: Mid: over 60,000 trained men, 38,000 of them under arms, at the start of the war (Scheina 2003 pp. 315-317, via the article). Low: the Cerro Leon camp was set up in March 1864 to train 30,000 men (George Thompson); high: about 64,000 men aged 16-50 in training by August 1864 (Velazquez Seiferheld), both via https://www.lanacion.com.py/gran-diario-domingo/2024/06/23/un-monumento-historico-que-lucha-contra-el-olvido/. The peacetime army before the February 1864 call-up was only about 7,500 (note 40 of the war article).

trainedReserves.note: Trained but not under arms: Scheina's 60,000 trained minus 38,000 under arms = 22,000 (mid). High: Salles 2003 p. 18 puts the army at 70,000-100,000 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguayan_War), 70,000 - 30,000 active (low) = 40,000. Low allows for recruits still untrained.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess: two artillery regiments (907 men in peacetime, note 40 of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguayan_War) expanded to four by 1864, crews of the 28 river steamers, arsenal and shipyard troops.

mobilizationRatio.note: Salles 2003 p. 18 (army of 70,000-100,000, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguayan_War) over the 420,000-450,000 population of Whigham and Potthast = 0.16-0.24. The militia took every able-bodied man, then boys and old men (note 40 of the article); Paraguay's mobilization was among the most complete of any 19th-century state.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Combat personnel (active - support, 34,000 at mid) x the infantry share at Cerro Leon in late December 1864: 10,958 infantry and 4,266 cavalry = 72% infantry (museum figures after von Horoch, https://www.lanacion.com.py/gran-diario-domingo/2024/06/23/un-monumento-historico-que-lucha-contra-el-olvido/). Low: the Cerro Leon infantry alone; high: 72% of 64,000.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: mostly old flintlock muskets against Allied percussion and rifled arms; the article calls the army poorly equipped (Salles 2003 p. 18).

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5 (conscripts with basic training). Evidence: most men called up in February 1864 and drilled for months at Cerro Leon and the regional depots; officers without training or experience (Salles 2003 p. 18).

count.note: Combat personnel x the 28% cavalry share at Cerro Leon in late December 1864 (4,266 of 15,224, https://www.lanacion.com.py/gran-diario-domingo/2024/06/23/un-monumento-historico-que-lucha-contra-el-olvido/). Low: the Cerro Leon cavalry alone; high: 28% of 64,000. Lancer and sabre regiments, counted as light horse.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: lances, sabres and few carbines.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: born horsemen of a cattle country, new to formation drill.

count.note: 400 cannons at the start of the war (Scheina 2003 pp. 315-317, via the article), many of them old smoothbore fortress guns at Humaita and the river batteries; low allows for unserviceable pieces.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25. Evidence: mostly obsolete smoothbores; a few modern pieces were cast later at the Asuncion arsenal.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: regular artillery regiments existed before the war (907 men in peacetime).

count.note: The purpose-built paddle gunboat Tacuari (named in the article); high counts one converted steamer as a line warship.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25. Evidence: an unarmoured wooden paddle steamer against Brazilian steam warships and, from 1865, ironclads.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5 minus. Evidence: small river navy with some foreign engineers.

count.note: 23 steamboats and five river-navigating ships (Scheina 2003 pp. 315-317, via the article) = 28, less the Tacuari counted as major; most were armed merchant river steamers. Low allows for unarmed transports.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25. Evidence: converted merchant steamers with a few guns each.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: river crews, no naval tradition; the fleet was destroyed at Riachuelo (June 1865).

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: Lopez took every decision himself and his officers had no training or experience (Salles 2003 p. 18, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguayan_War); the 1865 offensives into Corrientes and Rio Grande do Sul were lost piecemeal.

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75-1.0. Evidence: units fought on surrounded and to destruction for five years; draconian discipline.

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75-1.0. Evidence: national war against invasion; the population followed the army to the end (175,000-300,000 Paraguayan dead, war article infobox).

weapons.note: Anchor: 6 (1805, flintlock musket, field guns). Evidence: flintlock muskets and smoothbore cannon, a generation behind the percussion and rifled arms of 1864.

armor.note: Anchor: 6 (none). Evidence: no body armour, as in every army of the period.

ships.note: Anchor: 6-7. Evidence: steam paddle river craft, no ironclads.

fortification.note: Anchor: 6 (Vauban-type) toward 7 (trenches). Evidence: Humaita river batteries with a chain boom and long earthwork lines; the Allies needed until 1868 to take it.

logistics.note: Anchor: 6 (magazines + requisition). Evidence: river steamers on the Paraguay and a 72 km railway Asuncion-Paraguari; ox-carts elsewhere.

communications.note: Anchor: 6 (semaphore). Evidence: couriers and river steamers; whether the electric telegraph along the river was working in 1864 was not checked, hence grade D.

isr.note: Anchor: 5-6. Evidence: cavalry patrols and observation posts; no balloons (the Allies used them from 1867).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 has no Paraguay value before 1939 (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true). Analogues from the same file: Brazil 1864 = 971 (mid about that, Paraguay being a poor agrarian state); Latin America regional 1850 = 1,068, 1860 = 1,588 (high, scaled down for a landlocked economy); low 850 below Brazil. 2011 int$.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Mid is the 1864 mobilization year (wartime convention), low the peacetime share of a state that kept a small army but built an arsenal, shipyard and fortress from state yerba mate and timber monopolies.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. State arsenal and shipyard at Asuncion, the Ybycui ironworks and crafts; an agrarian and pastoral economy.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Self-sufficient in food (cattle, manioc, maize) with state estancias feeding the army; the army ate the herds down by 1868.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: cart roads around Asuncion and to the southern depots; the rivers carried most traffic.

railKm.note: Asuncion-Paraguari line, Paraguari at km 72, reached 6 October 1864 (uncited on the page). Low: the line to Pirayu/Cerro Leon opened in 1864 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rail_transport_in_Paraguay); service was suspended in 1865. Grade D, not C: the 72 km figure is uncited on the wiki mirror it comes from.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: river ports only (Asuncion, Pilar, Concepcion, Humaita landing); no sea coast, all trade passed Argentine waters on the Parana.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: the 28 river steamers and sailing craft were mostly taken into the navy; a few hundred tons each.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. The Corrientes and Uruguay River offensives of 1865 broke down at 200-400 km from the depots.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: oxen and horses of a cattle-raising country; no count found.

chokepoints: Humaita bend of the Paraguay River

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2-1.3: fortified river line, full population support, and marsh and disease that cost the Allied armies heavily; no great strategic depth, so below the full 1.3 row.

notes: Snapshot = December 1864, the mobilized Paraguayan army on the eve of the invasion of Mato Grosso that opened the War of the Triple Alliance. Personnel: men under arms (Scheina's 38,000 at mid) are activePersonnel, trained men at home are trainedReserves; the levy of every able man (boys and old men later) is the mobilizable pool. Population follows the post-1988 scholarship (Whigham and Potthast, Reber, Williams), not the old 1.3 million. Infantry/cavalry split from the Cerro Leon muster of late December 1864. Weakest values: GDP per capita (no Maddison series before 1939), the force split outside Cerro Leon, and the economy and logistics guesses. Territory = the world_1815 Paraguay polygon; includes is empty.
